```{r}
#| include: false
source("../../../book/R/setup.R")
```

Count how many plotting functions you know by name. Histogram, bar chart, box
plot, violin, density curve, area chart, step chart. Each one is a separate
thing to look up. Each has its own arguments in its own order. Learning one
teaches you almost nothing about the next.

That list is not a vocabulary. It is a phrase book.

Here is a different arrangement. The table is 142 countries, one row each, with a
life expectancy and an income:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

And this is a histogram of that life expectancy:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life)
```

Read it aloud: *given gapminder 2007, bars derived by binning,
x is life*. There is no `histogram` function in this library. There is a mark
called `bar`, a statistic called `bin`, and an operator `*` that derives one
from the other.

## Why that matters

Because now change one word.

The statistic stays. `bin` still divides life expectancy into intervals and
counts what lands in each. Only the shape drawn from those counts changes:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * bin + x(life)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + step * bin + x(life)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin + x(life)
```

Nothing was added to the library to make those work. There is no
`area_histogram`, no `step_histogram`, no documentation page for any of them. A
mark says what to draw and a statistic says what to draw it from, so any mark
that can show a number already knows how to show a count.

This is the whole idea, and it has a name in this project. The first of its nine
design laws is orthogonality: every compatible part combines with every other. A
rule you learn on one mark is true for every mark, or the library has failed
you.

## The same trick, one level up

Swap the statistic instead of the mark.

`density` estimates a distribution rather than counting one. Put it under
`ribbon`, which fills the space between two edges, and ask for one per
continent:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life)
```

That is a violin plot. It has no name in this grammar. Nobody added a violin;
the violin is what `ribbon * density` looks like.

Now use `area`, which fills from one edge down to the bottom:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + area * density + x(continent) + y(life)
```

A half violin, which in some libraries is a separate package. Here it is the
same sentence with a different mark, and no new word was needed.

## Changing a scale is changing a word

Here is income against life expectancy, one dot per country:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)
```

That picture is hard to read, and the reason is the data rather than the plot.
Most countries earn very little and a few earn very much more, so nearly every
dot is pressed against the left edge.

The usual fix is a log scale. Here it is:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + color(continent)
```

Look at what changed in the sentence. Not the mark, not the columns, not a
separate line added afterwards to adjust the axis. The scale is written on the
binding it belongs to, inside `x()`, because a scale is a fact about how one
column is read.

That placement is the point. The column and the way it is read cannot drift
apart, because they are written in the same pair of brackets. There is no second
statement further down that might name the wrong column, and nothing to remember
to change when you swap `gdp` for something else.

## It does not stop at histograms

Everything above uses five marks and two statistics. The vocabulary is small,
and so far it has only drawn ordinary plots. Here is what the same small vocabulary
does when you keep going.

Split one plot into many with `|`, which arranges rather than derives:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) | facet(continent)
```

Bend the plane into a circle with `polar()`, and a bar chart of wind directions
becomes a wind rose:

```{r}
data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction) + polar()
```

Use `nest()` to show the same shares as areas rather than as lengths, and a bar
chart becomes a treemap:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + y(population) + color(continent) + nest()
```

Add a third position and the plot stands up off the page. Drag this one:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + z(population) + color(continent)
```

Look at what those four sentences have in common. Each is the same shape as the
histogram at the top: a table, a mark, some positions, and at most one more
word. There is no new syntax in any of them, and no separate library for
circles or for three dimensions. `polar()` and `nest()` are words in
the same sentence, and `z` is one more position beside `x` and `y`.

That is what the small vocabulary is for. The words that get you a histogram
on your first day are the words that get you a wind rose and a rotating cube,
and there is no second thing to learn on the way.

## Every plot arrives with controls

Look underneath any plot on this page. There is a row of small boxes.

Two of them are magnifiers, and they look closer and wider. The frame gives you
back the whole picture. The camera saves what you are looking at as an image
file, large enough for a slide or a figure in a paper. The hand is not a button
at all, only a label telling you that you can drag the plot to move it. A box is
dimmed when there is nothing for it to do.

Every plot here has that row, including the plain histogram at the top of this
page. You did not ask for it. There is no word in the grammar that turns it on,
and that is deliberate: a word belongs in the grammar only if it changes what
the plot says about your data, and none of these change anything.

The plot in the cube has more, because it can do more. Drag it and it turns, and
a second button puts the angle back where it started. That is separate from the
button that puts the zoom back, so looking closer never costs you an angle you
spent time finding.

This is worth saying plainly. In most plotting libraries a finished plot is a
still image. Zooming into it, moving it, or saving a clean copy at a larger size
means reaching for a second library and writing more code. Here it is already
there, on a five line histogram, and you never wrote a line for it.

## Where the idea comes from

The discipline is borrowed from Hangeul, the Korean alphabet designed in 1443. A
learner can pick it up in a morning, and the reason is not that it has few
letters. English has few letters and still takes years to write well.

The reason is that its letters combine without exceptions. ㅋ is ㄱ with a stroke
added, and the stroke means the same thing everywhere it appears. You do not
memorize ㅋ. You derive it.

So `bar * bin` is not something to memorize either. The power was never in the
parts. It was in the regularity with which they join.

## What this costs you

The plots above show what works. This section says what does not.

This package is version 0.0.4 and the number means what it says. It is young. If
you use it for an experiment or a paper, you are taking a risk that you would not
take with a mature library. There are things ggplot2 draws that it cannot, and
[the book](https://psychometrician.github.io/gog-book/coverage.html) keeps a
dated list of exactly what those are, in both directions, so you do not have to
discover them yourself.

What it does have is a rule that a plot which draws is a plot that means what you
wrote. Ask for something the grammar cannot mean and you get a refusal that names
the fix. Nothing is accepted and then quietly dropped.

## What you can do

Four things, from the quickest to the one that takes real work.

### Read one chapter

The [book](https://psychometrician.github.io/gog-book/) is live: every plot in
it is drawn by the engine as the page builds, and none of them is a screenshot.
Start with [the grammar](https://psychometrician.github.io/gog-book/grammar.html),
which puts the entire vocabulary on one screen, or with
[transforms](https://psychometrician.github.io/gog-book/transforms.html), which
is where `bin` and `density` live.

### Install it and draw your own data

Three of the four bindings ship the engine inside the package, so there is
nothing else to set up.

```r
# R
install.packages("gog", repos = c("https://psychometrician.r-universe.dev",
                                  "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
```

```bash
# Python
pip install gog
```

```julia
# Julia
using Pkg; Pkg.add("GrammarOfGraphics")
```

```bash
# JavaScript
npm install grammar-of-graphics
```

### Check it against a tool you trust

This is the most useful thing anyone can do for this project right now, and here
is the reason. Three test harnesses draw every plot in the book from
Python, Julia and JavaScript and compare each against R. They prove the four
bindings agree with each other. They cannot prove that all four are right. A box
whose whiskers reached the wrong value would pass every one of those tests, four
times over, and the book would print it as though it were correct.

So draw a dataset you know well in gog and in something you already believe, put
the two side by side, and tell us where they differ.

### Report what breaks

[Issues are open](https://github.com/psychometrician/gog/issues). A refusal that
gave you no direction is a bug. So is a plot that drew when it should have
refused, which is the worse of the two and the harder to notice.

And if any of this is useful, pass it on to someone who spends their day looking
up chart functions.

One last thing about the name. *A Grammar of Graphics* shortens to **agog**,
which is English for eager, impatient to see what comes next. That is not luck.
It is also what using this feels like. You say what you want to see, and there
is a short wait before the engine shows you whether you said it right.

Be agog. Use gog.
